claim: CB2 agonists are potential analgesics void of psychotropic effects.
source: Cannabinoid CB2 receptor (CB2) agonists are potential analgesics void of psychotropic effects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about CB2 agonists, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Peripheral immune cells, neurons and glia express CB2.
source: Peripheral immune cells, neurons and glia express CB2; however, the involvement of CB2 from these cells in neuropathic pain remains unresolved.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, though the involvement in neuropathic pain is noted as unresolved.

claim: Constitutive deletion of CB2 disrupted JWH133-taking behavior in nerve-injured mice.
source: While constitutive deletion of CB2 disrupted JWH133-taking behavior, this behavior was not modified in monocyte-specific CB2 knockouts and was increased in mice defective in neuronal CB2 knockouts suggestive of increased spontaneous pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the self-administration experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: JWH133-taking behavior was not modified in monocyte-specific CB2 knockouts.
source: While constitutive deletion of CB2 disrupted JWH133-taking behavior, this behavior was not modified in monocyte-specific CB2 knockouts and was increased in mice defective in neuronal CB2 knockouts suggestive of increased spontaneous pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the self-administration experiments with LysM-Cre+ mice.

claim: JWH133-taking behavior was increased in neuronal CB2 knockouts, suggestive of increased spontaneous pain.
source: While constitutive deletion of CB2 disrupted JWH133-taking behavior, this behavior was not modified in monocyte-specific CB2 knockouts and was increased in mice defective in neuronal CB2 knockouts suggestive of increased spontaneous pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the self-administration experiments with Syn-Cre+ mice, with interpretation that increased drug-taking reflects increased spontaneous pain.

claim: CB2-positive lymphocytes infiltrated the injured nerve.
source: Interestingly, CB2-positive lymphocytes infiltrated the injured nerve and possible CB2transfer from immune cells to neurons was found.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data from bone marrow transplant experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: CB2 transfer from immune cells to neurons is possible.
source: Interestingly, CB2-positive lymphocytes infiltrated the injured nerve and possible CB2transfer from immune cells to neurons was found.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of GFP+ neurons in CB2-GFP bone marrow transplanted mice, suggesting transfer of CB2 from immune cells to neurons.

claim: Lymphocyte CB2 depletion exacerbated JWH133 self-administration.
source: Lymphocyte CB2depletion also exacerbated JWH133 self-administration and inhibited antinociception.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the anti-ICAM1 antibody treatment experiments.

claim: Lymphocyte CB2 depletion inhibited antinociception.
source: Lymphocyte CB2depletion also exacerbated JWH133 self-administration and inhibited antinociception.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the anti-ICAM1 antibody treatment experiments showing reduced JWH133 effects on mechanical nociception.

claim: Neuronal and lymphoid CB2 simultaneously protect against spontaneous and evoked neuropathic pain.
source: This work identifies a simultaneous activity of neuronal and lymphoid CB2that protects against spontaneous and evoked neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from conditional knockout and lymphocyte depletion experiments.

claim: CB2 agonists show efficacy in animal models of chronic inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
source: Cannabinoid CB2 receptor (CB2) agonists show efficacy in animal models of chronic inflammatory and neuropathic pain, suggesting that they may be effective inhibitors of persistent pain in humans (Bie et al., 2018; Maldonado et al., 2016; Shang and Tang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CB2 agonists may be effective inhibitors of persistent pain in humans.
source: Cannabinoid CB2 receptor (CB2) agonists show efficacy in animal models of chronic inflammatory and neuropathic pain, suggesting that they may be effective inhibitors of persistent pain in humans (Bie et al., 2018; Maldonado et al., 2016; Shang and Tang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on animal model data, supported by citations.

claim: Many preclinical studies assess reflexive-defensive reactions to evoked nociceptive stimuli and fail to take into account spontaneous pain.
source: However, many preclinical studies assess reflexive-defensive reactions to evoked nociceptive stimuli and fail to take into account spontaneous pain, one of the most prevalent symptoms of chronic pain conditions in humans (Backonja and Stacey, 2004; Mogil et al., 2010; Rice et al., 2018) that triggers coping responses such as analgesic consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a critique of existing methodologies.

claim: Spontaneous pain is one of the most prevalent symptoms of chronic pain conditions in humans.
source: However, many preclinical studies assess reflexive-defensive reactions to evoked nociceptive stimuli and fail to take into account spontaneous pain, one of the most prevalent symptoms of chronic pain conditions in humans (Backonja and Stacey, 2004; Mogil et al., 2010; Rice et al., 2018) that triggers coping responses such as analgesic consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Spontaneous pain triggers coping responses such as analgesic consumption.
source: However, many preclinical studies assess reflexive-defensive reactions to evoked nociceptive stimuli and fail to take into account spontaneous pain, one of the most prevalent symptoms of chronic pain conditions in humans (Backonja and Stacey, 2004; Mogil et al., 2010; Rice et al., 2018) that triggers coping responses such as analgesic consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about pain behavior.

claim: Conclusions drawn from animal models relying on evoked nociception may not translate into efficient pharmacotherapy in humans.
source: As a consequence, conclusions drawn from animal models relying on evoked nociception may not translate into efficient pharmacotherapy in humans (Huang et al., 2019; Mogil, 2009; Percie du Sert and Rice, 2014), which underlines the need to apply more sophisticated animal models with clear translational value.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research discussing translational challenges.

claim: There is a need to apply more sophisticated animal models with clear translational value.
source: As a consequence, conclusions drawn from animal models relying on evoked nociception may not translate into efficient pharmacotherapy in humans (Huang et al., 2019; Mogil, 2009; Percie du Sert and Rice, 2014), which underlines the need to apply more sophisticated animal models with clear translational value.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the limitations of current models, supported by citations.

claim: Operant paradigms in which animals voluntarily self-administer analgesic compounds can provide high translatability.
source: Operant paradigms in which animals voluntarily self-administer analgesic compounds can provide high translatability and also identify in the same experimental approach potential addictive properties of the drugs (Mogil, 2009; Mogil et al., 2010; O'Connor et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on operant paradigms.

claim: Operant paradigms can identify potential addictive properties of drugs.
source: Operant paradigms in which animals voluntarily self-administer analgesic compounds can provide high translatability and also identify in the same experimental approach potential addictive properties of the drugs (Mogil, 2009; Mogil et al., 2010; O'Connor et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on operant paradigms.

claim: A previous work using CB2 agonist AM1241 showed drug-taking behavior in nerve-injured rats and not in sham-operated animals.
source: In this line, a previous work using a CB2 agonist, AM1241, showed drug-taking behavior in nerve-injured rats and not in sham-operated animals, suggesting spontaneous pain relief and lack of abuse potential of CB2agonists (Gutierrez et al., 2011), although the possible cell populations and mechanisms involved remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: AM1241 drug-taking behavior suggests spontaneous pain relief and lack of abuse potential of CB2 agonists.
source: In this line, a previous work using a CB2 agonist, AM1241, showed drug-taking behavior in nerve-injured rats and not in sham-operated animals, suggesting spontaneous pain relief and lack of abuse potential of CB2agonists (Gutierrez et al., 2011), although the possible cell populations and mechanisms involved remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited study's results.

claim: The cell populations and mechanisms involved in AM1241 effects remain unknown.
source: In this line, a previous work using a CB2 agonist, AM1241, showed drug-taking behavior in nerve-injured rats and not in sham-operated animals, suggesting spontaneous pain relief and lack of abuse potential of CB2agonists (Gutierrez et al., 2011), although the possible cell populations and mechanisms involved remain unknown.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge from previous research.

claim: AM1241 has off-target effects on anandamide reuptake, calcium channels and serotonin, histamine and kappa opioid receptors.
source: In addition, a recent multicenter study demonstrated off-target effects of this compound on anandamide reuptake, calcium channels and serotonin, histamine and kappa opioid receptors (Soethoudt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a multicenter study.

claim: CB2 is the main cannabinoid receptor in peripheral immune cells.
source: CB2, the main cannabinoid receptors in peripheral immune cells (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2007; Schmöle et al., 2015a), are found in monocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes, and their expression increases in conditions of active inflammation (Schmöle et al., 2015b; Shang and Tang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CB2 is found in monocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes.
source: CB2, the main cannabinoid receptors in peripheral immune cells (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2007; Schmöle et al., 2015a), are found in monocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes, and their expression increases in conditions of active inflammation (Schmöle et al., 2015b; Shang and Tang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CB2 expression increases in conditions of active inflammation.
source: CB2, the main cannabinoid receptors in peripheral immune cells (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2007; Schmöle et al., 2015a), are found in monocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes, and their expression increases in conditions of active inflammation (Schmöle et al., 2015b; Shang and Tang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of CB2 in the nervous system was thought to be restricted to microglia and limited to pathological conditions or intense neuronal activity.
source: The presence of CB2 in the nervous system was thought to be restricted to microglia and limited to pathological conditions or intense neuronal activity (Manzanares et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes previous understanding in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Recent studies using electrophysiological approaches and tissue-specific genetic deletion revealed functional CB2 in neurons.
source: However, recent studies using electrophysiological approaches and tissue-specific genetic deletion revealed functional CB2 also in neurons, where they modulate dopamine-related behaviors (Zhang et al., 2014) and basic neurotransmission (Quraishi and Paladini, 2016; Stempel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research studies.

claim: Neuronal CB2 modulates dopamine-related behaviors.
source: However, recent studies using electrophysiological approaches and tissue-specific genetic deletion revealed functional CB2 also in neurons, where they modulate dopamine-related behaviors (Zhang et al., 2014) and basic neurotransmission (Quraishi and Paladini, 2016; Stempel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Neuronal CB2 modulates basic neurotransmission.
source: However, recent studies using electrophysiological approaches and tissue-specific genetic deletion revealed functional CB2 also in neurons, where they modulate dopamine-related behaviors (Zhang et al., 2014) and basic neurotransmission (Quraishi and Paladini, 2016; Stempel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: The specific contribution of immune and neuronal CB2 to the development of chronic pathological pain has not yet been established.
source: Remarkably, the specific contribution of immune and neuronal CB2 to the development of chronic pathological pain has not yet been established.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Nerve-injured mice exposed to the high dose of JWH133 (0.3 mg/kg/inf) showed higher active responses than sham-operated mice receiving the same treatment.
source: Conversely, nerve-injured mice exposed to the high dose of JWH133 (0.3 mg/kg/inf) showed higher active responses than sham-operated mice receiving the same treatment (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The operant behavior of sham-operated mice exposed to JWH133 was not different from that of sham mice exposed to vehicle.
source: As expected, the operant behavior of sham-operated mice exposed to JWH133 was not different from that of sham mice exposed to vehicle, suggesting absence of reinforcing effects of the CB2 agonist in mice without pain (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: JWH133 has no reinforcing effects in mice without pain.
source: As expected, the operant behavior of sham-operated mice exposed to JWH133 was not different from that of sham mice exposed to vehicle, suggesting absence of reinforcing effects of the CB2 agonist in mice without pain (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing no difference in operant behavior between sham mice receiving JWH133 or vehicle.

claim: The number of nose pokes on the inactive sensor was similar among the groups, indicating absence of locomotor effects of the surgery or the pharmacological treatments.
source: The number of nose pokes on the inactive sensor was similar among the groups, indicating absence of locomotor effects of the surgery or the pharmacological treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and represents an interpretation of the inactive nose poke data.

claim: Operant JWH133 self-administration was selectively associated to the neuropathic condition.
source: Thus, operant JWH133 self-administration was selectively associated to the neuropathic condition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing increased self-administration only in nerve-injured mice.

claim: All nerve-injured mice developed heat and mechanical hypersensitivity in the ipsilateral paw before treatment with the CB2 agonist.
source: Before the treatment with the CB2 agonist, all nerve-injured mice developed heat and mechanical hypersensitivity in the ipsilateral paw (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After self-administration, mice exposed to JWH133 showed a significant reduction in heat hypersensitivity.
source: After self-administration (shaded area, Figure 1C) mice exposed to JWH133 showed a significant reduction in heat hypersensitivity (Figure 1C, day 18, ipsilateral paw), although the alleviation of mechanical hypersensitivity did not reach statistical significance in this experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The alleviation of mechanical hypersensitivity by JWH133 did not reach statistical significance in the dose-response experiment.
source: After self-administration (shaded area, Figure 1C) mice exposed to JWH133 showed a significant reduction in heat hypersensitivity (Figure 1C, day 18, ipsilateral paw), although the alleviation of mechanical hypersensitivity did not reach statistical significance in this experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Anxiety-like behavior was enhanced in nerve-injured mice treated with vehicle.
source: Anxiety-like behavior was enhanced in nerve-injured mice treated with vehicle, as these mice visited less frequently the open arms of the elevated plus maze (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nerve-injured mice repeatedly exposed to the high dose of JWH133 did not show enhanced anxiety-like behavior.
source: This emotional response was absent in nerve-injured mice repeatedly exposed to the high dose of JWH133 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The high dose of JWH133 elicited a drug-taking behavior selectively associated to spontaneous pain relief.
source: Therefore, the high dose of JWH133 elicited a drug-taking behavior selectively associated to spontaneous pain relief, and had efficacy limiting the pronociceptive effects of the nerve injury and its emotional-like consequences.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the combined experimental data on self-administration, nociception, and anxiety-like behavior.

claim: JWH133 had efficacy limiting the pronociceptive effects of the nerve injury and its emotional-like consequences.
source: Therefore, the high dose of JWH133 elicited a drug-taking behavior selectively associated to spontaneous pain relief, and had efficacy limiting the pronociceptive effects of the nerve injury and its emotional-like consequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on nociception and anxiety-like behavior.

claim: JWH133 has been recently recommended as a selective CB2 agonist due to its high selectivity for this receptor.
source: JWH133 has been recently recommended as a selective CB2 agonist to study the role of CB2 in biological and disease processes due to its high selectivity for this receptor (Soethoudt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: CB2 KO mice showed a significant disruption of JWH133-taking behavior on the last sessions of the drug self-administration period.
source: CB2 KO mice showed a significant disruption of JWH133-taking behavior on the last sessions of the drug self-administration period (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overall discrimination between the active and inactive sensors was significantly blunted in CB2 KO mice.
source: Overall discrimination between the active and inactive sensors was also significantly blunted in CB2 KO mice (Source Data File) and inactive nose pokes were similar in both groups of mice, indicating absence of genotype effect on locomotion (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and the Source Data File.

claim: Inactive nose pokes were similar in CB2 KO and wild-type mice, indicating absence of genotype effect on locomotion.
source: Overall discrimination between the active and inactive sensors was also significantly blunted in CB2 KO mice (Source Data File) and inactive nose pokes were similar in both groups of mice, indicating absence of genotype effect on locomotion (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and represents an interpretation of the inactive nose poke data.

claim: The disruption of drug-taking behavior in CB2 KO mice was accompanied by an inhibition of JWH133 effects on nociceptive and affective behavior.
source: The disruption of drug-taking behavior shown in CB2 KO mice was accompanied by an inhibition of JWH133 effects on nociceptive and affective behavior (Figure 2B, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: CB2 KO and C57BL/6J mice developed similar thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in the injured paw.
source: CB2 KO and C57BL/6J mice developed similar thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in the injured paw (Figure 2B, day 6, Ipsilateral paw), although CB2 KO mice also developed hypersensitivity in the contralateral paw, as previously described (Racz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CB2 KO mice developed hypersensitivity in the contralateral paw.
source: CB2 KO and C57BL/6J mice developed similar thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in the injured paw (Figure 2B, day 6, Ipsilateral paw), although CB2 KO mice also developed hypersensitivity in the contralateral paw, as previously described (Racz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to a previous study.

claim: C57BL/6J mice showed significant recovery of thermal and mechanical thresholds after JWH133 self-administration.
source: While C57BL/6J mice showed significant recovery of thermal and mechanical thresholds after JWH133 self-administration (Figure 2B, day 18), CB2 KO mice showed no effects of the treatment on mechanical sensitivity (Figure 2B, day 18, Mechanical) and a partial recovery of the thresholds to heat stimulation (Figure 2B, day 18, Heat).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CB2 KO mice showed no effects of JWH133 treatment on mechanical sensitivity.
source: While C57BL/6J mice showed significant recovery of thermal and mechanical thresholds after JWH133 self-administration (Figure 2B, day 18), CB2 KO mice showed no effects of the treatment on mechanical sensitivity (Figure 2B, day 18, Mechanical) and a partial recovery of the thresholds to heat stimulation (Figure 2B, day 18, Heat).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CB2 KO mice showed partial recovery of the thresholds to heat stimulation after JWH133 treatment.
source: While C57BL/6J mice showed significant recovery of thermal and mechanical thresholds after JWH133 self-administration (Figure 2B, day 18), CB2 KO mice showed no effects of the treatment on mechanical sensitivity (Figure 2B, day 18, Mechanical) and a partial recovery of the thresholds to heat stimulation (Figure 2B, day 18, Heat).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nerve-injured C57BL/6J mice showed less anxiety-like behavior after JWH133 self-administration than CB2 KO mice.
source: Likewise, nerve-injured C57BL/6J mice showed less anxiety-like behavior after JWH133 self-administration than CB2 KO mice (Figure 2C), suggesting that these anxiolytic-like effects of JWH133 are mediated by CB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The anxiolytic-like effects of JWH133 are mediated by CB2.
source: Likewise, nerve-injured C57BL/6J mice showed less anxiety-like behavior after JWH133 self-administration than CB2 KO mice (Figure 2C), suggesting that these anxiolytic-like effects of JWH133 are mediated by CB2.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data comparing anxiety-like behavior in CB2 KO and wild-type mice.

claim: CB2 KO mice showed reduced drug-taking behavior accompanied by blunted inhibition of JWH133 effects on mechanical nociception and anxiety-like behavior, confirming mediation of these effects by CB2.
source: Hence, CB2 KO mice showed reduced drug-taking behavior accompanied by blunted inhibition of JWH133 effects on mechanical nociception and anxiety-like behavior, confirming mediation of these effects by CB2.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the combined experimental data in CB2 KO mice.

claim: JWH133 has effects interacting with TRPA1.
source: JWH133 has shown effects interacting with the Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin1 (TRPA1) (Soethoudt et al., 2017), a receptor needed for thermal pain perception (Vandewauw et al., 2018), that could also participate in other nociceptive responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TRPA1 is a receptor needed for thermal pain perception.
source: JWH133 has shown effects interacting with the Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin1 (TRPA1) (Soethoudt et al., 2017), a receptor needed for thermal pain perception (Vandewauw et al., 2018), that could also participate in other nociceptive responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: JWH133 had similar effects on mechanical hypersensitivity in TRPA1 KO and WT mice.
source: We observed similar effects of JWH133 inhibiting mechanical hypersensitivity in TRPA1 KO and WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TRPA1 KO mice showed a prominent inhibition of neuropathic thermal hypersensitivity.
source: Interestingly, TRPA1 KO mice showed a prominent inhibition of neuropathic thermal hypersensitivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The results on mechanical sensitivity suggest that JWH133 effects are not due to an interaction with the TRPA1 receptor.
source: Thus, the results on mechanical sensitivity suggest that these effects are not due to an interaction of the drug with the TRPA1 receptor.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing similar JWH133 effects in TRPA1 KO and WT mice.

claim: At least the CB2 receptor is involved in the inhibitory effect of JWH133 on thermal hyperalgesia.
source: The lack of thermal hypersensitivity observed in the TRPA1 KO mice may occlude possible JWH133 effects on neuropathic thermal hyperalgesia through TRPA1; however, a significant effect of JWH133 was observed in both strains after the nerve injury, suggesting that at least the CB2 receptor is involved in the inhibitory effect on thermal hyperalgesia.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing JWH133 effects in both TRPA1 KO and WT mice.

claim: Syn-Cre+ mice showed increased active operant responding for JWH133.
source: Syn-Cre+ mice showed increased active operant responding for JWH133 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting increased spontaneous pain and possible decrease of drug effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased JWH133 self-administration in Syn-Cre+ mice suggests increased spontaneous pain and possible decrease of drug effects.
source: Syn-Cre+ mice showed increased active operant responding for JWH133 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting increased spontaneous pain and possible decrease of drug effects.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data on self-administration in Syn-Cre+ mice.

claim: LysM-Cre+ mice did not show significant alteration of drug-taking behavior.
source: On the other hand, LysM-Cre+ mice did not show significant alteration of drug-taking behavior (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Data from the drug self-administration experiments showed persistence of drug effects in the different genotypes and increased self-administration in mice lacking neuronal CB2.
source: Thus, data from the drug self-administration experiments showed persistence of drug effects in the different genotypes and increased self-administration in mice lacking neuronal CB2, suggestive of increased spontaneous pain.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data on self-administration in conditional knockout mice.

claim: The three mouse lines (Cre Neg, Syn-Cre+, LysM-Cre+) showed similar evoked responses to nociceptive stimulation after nerve injury.
source: The three mouse lines showed similar evoked responses to nociceptive stimulation after nerve injury (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A slight but significant impairment on the effect of JWH133 on mechanical sensitivity was found in Syn-Cre+ mice.
source: A slight but significant impairment on the effect of JWH133 on mechanical sensitivity was found in Syn-Cre+ mice (Figure 3C) in spite of the increased JWH133 consumption, compatible with reduced efficacy of JWH133 in this mouse strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B (likely a typo in the manuscript, should be 3B based on context).

claim: The impairment of JWH133 effects on mechanical sensitivity in Syn-Cre+ mice is compatible with reduced efficacy of JWH133 in this mouse strain.
source: A slight but significant impairment on the effect of JWH133 on mechanical sensitivity was found in Syn-Cre+ mice (Figure 3C) in spite of the increased JWH133 consumption, compatible with reduced efficacy of JWH133 in this mouse strain.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data on mechanical nociception in Syn-Cre+ mice.

claim: The assessment of anxiety-like behavior did not reveal apparent differences among the three genotypes (Cre Neg, Syn-Cre+, LysM-Cre+).
source: The assessment of anxiety-like behavior did not reveal apparent differences among the three genotypes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increased JWH133 consumption in Syn-Cre+ mice was not reflected in increased anxiolysis.
source: Thus, the increased JWH133 consumption observed in Syn-Cre+ mice was not reflected in increased anxiolysis and JWH133 antinociceptive effects were blunted, suggesting partial involvement of neuronal CB2 in the development of spontaneous and evoked neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data on anxiety-like behavior in Syn-Cre+ mice.

claim: JWH133 antinociceptive effects were blunted in Syn-Cre+ mice, suggesting partial involvement of neuronal CB2 in the development of spontaneous and evoked neuropathic pain.
source: Thus, the increased JWH133 consumption observed in Syn-Cre+ mice was not reflected in increased anxiolysis and JWH133 antinociceptive effects were blunted, suggesting partial involvement of neuronal CB2 in the development of spontaneous and evoked neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the combined experimental data in Syn-Cre+ mice.

claim: No significant differences were observed between Nav1.8-Cre+ and Cre Neg mice in mechanical or thermal sensitivity after JWH133 treatment.
source: No significant differences were observed between both genotypes in mechanical or thermal sensitivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) revealing that CB2 primarily expressed in nociceptors were not involved in the antinociceptive effects of JWH133.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CB2 primarily expressed in nociceptors were not involved in the antinociceptive effects of JWH133.
source: No significant differences were observed between both genotypes in mechanical or thermal sensitivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) revealing that CB2 primarily expressed in nociceptors were not involved in the antinociceptive effects of JWH133.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data in Nav1.8-Cre+ mice.

claim: A significant infiltration of non-neuronal GFP+ cells was revealed in nerve injured CB2-GFP BMT mice (~30 cells/mm2).
source: A significant infiltration of non-neuronal GFP+ cells was revealed in nerve injured CB2-GFP BMT mice (~30 cells/mm2, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that CB2 -expressing cells invaded the injured nerve.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CB2-expressing cells invaded the injured nerve.
source: A significant infiltration of non-neuronal GFP+ cells was revealed in nerve injured CB2-GFP BMT mice (~30 cells/mm2, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that CB2 -expressing cells invaded the injured nerve.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the immunohistochemical data showing GFP+ cells in the dorsal root ganglia.

claim: Nearly 60% of infiltrating macrophages were found to be GFP+.
source: Immunostaining to identify these cell types revealed co-localization with macrophage and lymphocyte markers. Nearly 60% of infiltrating macrophages and around 40% of the lymphocytes were found to be GFP+ (Figure 4B, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Around 40% of the infiltrating lymphocytes were found to be GFP+.
source: Immunostaining to identify these cell types revealed co-localization with macrophage and lymphocyte markers. Nearly 60% of infiltrating macrophages and around 40% of the lymphocytes were found to be GFP+ (Figure 4B, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A significant percentage of neurons was found to express GFP in CB2-GFP BMT mice.
source: Surprisingly, a significant percentage of neurons was also found to express GFP in CB2-GFP BMT mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The percentage of GFP+ neurons was higher in nerve-injured mice (~4% of total neurons) than in sham-operated animals (~2%).
source: The percentage of GFP+ neurons was higher in nerve-injured mice (~4% of total neurons) than in sham-operated animals (~2%, Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: GFP in neurons could only come from bone-marrow transplanted cells, suggesting a transfer of CB2 from bone-marrow derived cells to neurons.
source: Since GFP could only come from bone-marrow transplanted cells, this finding suggests a transfer of CB2 from bone-marrow derived cells to neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental design and the observation of GFP+ neurons in bone marrow transplanted mice.

claim: Nerve injury facilitated the invasion of affected ganglia by CB2-positive immune cells.
source: Hence, nerve injury facilitated the invasion of affected ganglia by CB2-positive immune cells and promoted a neuronal GFP expression compatible with transfer of CB2 from immune cells to neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the immunohistochemical data showing increased infiltration after nerve injury.

claim: Nerve injury promoted a neuronal GFP expression compatible with transfer of CB2 from immune cells to neurons.
source: Hence, nerve injury facilitated the invasion of affected ganglia by CB2-positive immune cells and promoted a neuronal GFP expression compatible with transfer of CB2 from immune cells to neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing increased GFP+ neurons after nerve injury in bone marrow transplanted mice.

claim: Anti-ICAM1 significantly increased active nose poking to obtain i.v. JWH133 without altering the inactive nose poking.
source: Mice under treatment with anti-ICAM1 or with the control IgG were exposed to JWH133 self-administration. Instead of reducing the intake of the CB2 agonist, anti-ICAM1 significantly increased active nose poking to obtain i.v. JWH133 without altering the inactive nose poking (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting increased spontaneous pain.

claim: CB2 agonists are void of reinforcing effects in animals without pain, suggesting the absence of abuse liability.
source: Our results provide evidence that the effect of the CB2 agonist is sufficient to promote drug-taking behavior in nerve-injured mice for alleviation of spontaneous pain, but it is void of reinforcing effects in animals without pain, suggesting the absence of abuse liability.

claim: Current available agents for neuropathic pain treatment have reduced efficacy and often show addictive properties in humans and rodents.
source: This absence of reinforcement adds value to the modulation of pain through CB2 agonists, since current available agents for neuropathic pain treatment have reduced efficacy and often show addictive properties in humans and rodents (Attal and Bouhassira, 2015; Bonnet and Scherbaum, 2017; Bura et al., 2018; Finnerup et al., 2015; Hipólito et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2011).

claim: CB2 agonists would be of interest for preventing neuropathic pain development.
source: Therefore, CB2 agonists would be of interest for preventing neuropathic pain development and the potential trials to evaluate this effect should consider starting CB2 agonist treatment before or shortly after the induction of neuropathic insults, as in our study, in contrast to the treatment strategies used in previous clinical trials.
evidence: This claim is speculation about clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: The identification of a cannabinoid agonist simultaneously targeting the behavioral traits and the multiple cell types involved in the pathophysiology of chronic neuropathic pain acquires special relevance in a moment in which the absence of efficient analgesics void of abuse liability has become a major burden for public health.
